title: The Schrödinger Equation is an Eigenvalue Problem
lead: When an operator returns its function multiplied by a constant, the function is an eigenfunction and the constant its eigenvalue. Every measurable quantity has an operator whose eigenvalues are the values a measurement can give, and the operator of the energy is the Hamiltonian of the Schrödinger equation.
objectives: To recognize that each quantum mechanical observable is determined by solve by an eigenvalue problem with different operators for different observable
Confirm if a specific wavefunction is an eigenfunction of a specific operation and extract the corresponding obserable (the eigenvalue)
To recognize that the Schrödinger equation, just like all measurable, is also an eigenvalue problem with the eigenvalue ascribed to total energy
Identity and manipulate several common quantum mechanical operators
notes: Adapted from Hanson, Harvey, Sweeney and Zielinski's Quantum States of Atoms and Molecules under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
exercise_notes: Exercise 3.3.1 and its key are the book's; the key's kinetic-energy eigenvalue is corrected in a note. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI.

exercises.prompt: Are $\kpsi = M e^{-b\kx}$ functions eigenstates of linear momentum and kinetic energy (or neither or both)?

answer.solution: $\kpsi$ is an eigenstate of linear momentum with a eigenvalue of $bi\hbar$ and also an eigenstate of kinetic energy with an eigenvalue of $b^2$.

footnotes.html: Only the time-independent equation, $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$, is an eigenvalue equation. The time-dependent one has the time derivative $i\hbar\,\partial\Psi/\partial t$ on its right side, not a constant times $\Psi$.
The Hamiltonian is the right-hand side of Equation 3.3.19.
$\phi_i$ names the eigenstates of the operator, not the operator itself.
The derivative brings down $-i\hbar(-i/\hbar) = -1$, so the momentum is $p_x = -1$; the constant $N$ cancels from both sides.
